html:
Conic sections of a cone
All four printed cuts are shown at once. Pick one to make it the active cut, then steepen its plane with the slider.
Named conic cut (active)
Section: circle — closed
Slant of the cone = 68.2°. Below it the cut closes (circle / ellipse); exactly at it the cut escapes (parabola); above it, hyperbola.
Guided demo
Drag in the figure to orbit: the dashed “lines” are really flat planes, and each shaded section is a genuine 2‑D curve lying in its plane. Click a shaded section for an explanation.
⚠ Figure failed to load

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional drawing of a right circular cone, shaded in translucent teal with its apex at the top and an elliptical base at the bottom, cut by four dashed lines that each mark a different slicing plane. Near the apex a short, nearly horizontal dashed segment crossing a lightly shaded band is labeled 'Circle'. Below it a dashed line tilted modestly from horizontal passes through both sides of the cone and is labeled 'Ellipse'. A steeper dashed line runs from the upper left side of the cone down through the base and carries the label 'Parabola'. The fourth dashed line is nearly vertical, dropping through the right portion of the cone to the base, and is labeled 'Hyperbola'. Each cut has a correspondingly shaded region rendered inside the translucent solid, so the section surface itself is visible rather than just the cutting line, and all four labels are stacked along the right edge. Steepening the cut progressively from horizontal to vertical is the entire visual argument: one surface yields all four curves depending only on the inclination of the plane. The drawing collects the family of paths that an inverse-square force allows, the closed circle and ellipse alongside the open parabola and hyperbola.

elements: right circular cone, apex at top, translucent teal shell with vertical gradient highlight
elliptical base disk of the cone (darker teal, seen in shallow perspective from slightly above)
faint vertical cone axis from apex to base center
cutting plane 1: nearly horizontal dashed line near the apex — Circle cut
cutting plane 2: modestly tilted dashed line lower down, entering left side and exiting right side — Ellipse cut
cutting plane 3: steep dashed line from upper-left slant of the cone down through the base — Parabola cut
cutting plane 4: near-vertical dashed line dropping through the right portion of the cone to the base — Hyperbola cut
shaded section surface (interior intersection region) for each of the four cuts, visible through the translucent solid
leader/label text stacked along the right edge: 'Circle', 'Ellipse', 'Parabola', 'Hyperbola'
short leader ticks connecting each label to its dashed cut line

interactions.label: Cutting-plane tilt from horizontal (°)
interactions.teaches: One cone produces the whole conic family: as the plane steepens past horizontal the section stretches from circle to ellipse, becomes an unbounded parabola exactly when the plane is parallel to the cone's slant side (~68°), and opens into a hyperbola beyond that.

interactions.label: Named conic cut
interactions.teaches: Which dashed line in the original figure corresponds to which orbit shape, and that circle/ellipse are closed bounded sections while parabola/hyperbola are open and run off the cone.
The dashed 'lines' are really flat planes slicing a solid of revolution; rotating shows the section as a genuine 2D curve lying in that plane rather than an outline drawn on the surface.

demo_steps.title: Circle — plane perpendicular to the axis
demo_steps.narration: A horizontal plane near the apex cuts a small closed circle. Every point of the section is the same distance from the cone's axis.

demo_steps.title: Ellipse — tilt the plane modestly
demo_steps.narration: Tilting the plane about 25° still lets it exit through both sides of the cone, so the section closes — but now as a stretched ellipse.

demo_steps.title: Parabola — plane parallel to the slant side
demo_steps.narration: At the critical tilt (~68°, matching the cone's slant) the plane never catches the far wall. The curve stops closing and escapes: a parabola, the marginally unbound orbit.

demo_steps.title: Hyperbola — steeper than the slant
demo_steps.narration: Past the slant angle the plane cuts a single branch that opens ever wider — the hyperbolic, definitively unbound trajectory.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cone: apex at (0, +2.2, 0), base circle radius 1.6 centered at (0, -1.8, 0), height 4.0; half-angle = atan(1.6/4.0) ≈ 21.8°, so the slant side makes 68.2° with the horizontal — that is the exact parabola threshold for the slider. Axis is vertical (+Y screen-up); base ellipse foreshortened by the ~12° camera elevation. Cutting planes all contain a horizontal line perpendicular to the viewing axis and tilt about it: Circle plane at y≈+1.3 (tilt 0°, section radius ≈0.36); Ellipse plane at y≈+0.6, tilt ≈25°; Parabola plane tilt 68.2° passing through the upper-LEFT slant and exiting the base near the left-front rim; Hyperbola plane tilt ≈85° offset to the RIGHT of the axis by x≈+0.55, dropping to the base. Colors: cone body translucent teal #7FBFBF with a lighter vertical highlight band #BFE0DE down the left-center and a darker rim #3E8C8C; base disk #4F9E9E with darker ellipse edge #2F7676; section surfaces a desaturated gray-teal #6E9494 at ~0.55 opacity; cut lines black dashed (dash 0.12, gap 0.10, width ~1.5px); labels black sans-serif, stacked at the right edge at descending heights y ≈ +2.0 (Circle), +1.5 (Ellipse), +0.9 (Parabola), +0.1 (Hyperbola), each with a short leader tick to its dashed line.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the cone as a ConeGeometry (radialSegments 64, openEnded false) with MeshPhysicalMaterial, transparent true, opacity ~0.45, depthWrite false, side: THREE.DoubleSide so interior walls read through the shell. Compute the section curve analytically: intersect the plane with the cone x²+z² = (r/h)²·(apexY − y)² and sample it as a polyline, then triangulate (fan for closed conics, clipped strip for parabola/hyperbola) into a filled mesh so the section surface is visible, not just the line. Draw the dashed cut lines with LineDashedMaterial and call computeLineDistances() after every slider update. Unselected cuts fade to opacity ~0.12 with gray lines; the selected cut's plane, section fill, and label render at full opacity with an accent outline. Labels via CSS2DRenderer anchored to fixed screen-right positions so stacking survives orbiting. Clamp orbit elevation to roughly −5°…55° to keep the apex-up reading of the figure.

authoredContext:
One of the real triumphs of Newton’s law of universal gravitation, with the force proportional to the inverse of the distance squared, is that when it is combined with his second law, the solution for the path of any satellite is a conic section. Every path taken by m is one of the four conic sections: a circle or an ellipse for bound or closed orbits, or a parabola or hyperbola for unbounded or open orbits. These conic sections are shown in the figure.

All motion caused by an inverse square force is one of the four conic sections and is determined by the energy and direction of the moving body.

A cone and its conic sections is shown. At the top a horizontal cut is shaded and a dashed line shown across the shading. This section is labeled circle. Below this a diagonal cut and line are shown. The line and cut intersect the sides of the cone. This section is labeled ellipse. Next is a diagonal cut and line that intersect the sides and the bottom of the cone and are labeled parabola. The last section is a vertical line and shaded cut labeled hyperbola

If the total energy is negative, then 0≤e<1, and the equation represents a bound or closed orbit of either an ellipse or a circle, where e=0. [You can see from the equation that for e=0, r=α, and hence the radius is constant.] For ellipses, the eccentricity is related to how oblong the ellipse appears. A circle has zero eccentricity, whereas a very long, drawn-out ellipse has an eccentricity near one.

Conic sections of a cone
Section: circle
Slant of the cone = 68.2°. Below it the cut closes; exactly at it the cut escapes (parabola); above it, hyperbola.
Named conic cut
Guided demo
Drag in the figure to orbit: the dashed “lines” are really flat planes, and each shaded section is a genuine 2‑D curve lying in its plane.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: In the default view only the Circle cut is drawn at full strength; the Ellipse, Parabola and Hyperbola traces and shaded sections are faded to ~0.12–0.45 opacity and are nearly invisible, whereas the source shows all four dashed cut lines and all four shaded section regions simultaneously at equal weight.
The three non-active labels are rendered in pale grey (#9aa5a5) instead of the uniform black text of the source, weakening the four-way comparison the figure is built around.
The dark grey shaded conic regions inside the cone (a prominent feature of the source, giving the sense of curved surfaces slicing through the solid) are barely perceptible in the generated render.

Leader/dash lines extend well outside the cone silhouette (e.g. the long horizontal dash running far to the right of the apex for 'Circle'), longer and more prominent than the short dashed leaders in the source.

The source's soft vertical light-band/gradient shading on the cone body is only weakly reproduced; the generated cone reads as a flat uniform translucent teal with a visible darker back-facing region.
evaluation.notes: Geometrically and conceptually sound analytic conic sections with an excellent set of interactions (tilt slider, four named cuts, guided demo), but the default render de-emphasises three of the four cuts so heavily that the side-by-side four-conic composition of the source is largely lost at a glance.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are sound; the issues are rendering-level (opacity of inactive cuts, label coloring, shading, overlong leader lines) that require implementation tweaks rather than a new plan.

discrepancies: The circle cut is drawn as a full-width horizontal dashed line crossing well outside both sides of the cone, whereas the source shows only a short dashed segment at the small circle near the apex plus a leader to the label.

The shaded conic sections are much fainter than in the source, where the ellipse/parabola/hyperbola regions read as distinctly darker teal patches; in the render the ellipse and hyperbola faces are barely discernible.
The cone's surface shading is flat compared with the source's strong vertical light-stripe/gradient highlight down the left-centre of the shell.

Label placement differs: the source clusters the four labels tightly at the upper right near the apex, while the generated figure spreads them far down the right edge with long leader dashes, so 'Hyperbola' sits mid-cone rather than near the top.
In the source the parabola and hyperbola dashed traces run all the way off the bottom of the figure past the base ellipse; in the render they stop just at/near the base plane.
evaluation.notes: A genuinely 3D, analytically correct conic-sections cone with excellent interactivity (conic selector, tilt slider with correct 68.2° slant threshold, show-all toggle, guided demo, clickable sections); main weaknesses are the washed-out section fills and flat cone shading plus an over-extended circle trace and label stack that drifts from the source's tight upper-right annotation cluster.
action_items: Increase opacity/contrast of the four section fills (and their outlines) so each cut reads as a distinct darker patch like the printed figure.
Shorten the circle cut's dashed trace to a small segment at the apex-side circle and rely on a short leader to its label, as in the source.
Add a vertical light-stripe gradient (or stronger specular/emissive band) on the cone shell to reproduce the source's shaded highlight.
Raise and tighten the label column so the four names stack near the upper right (Circle at apex level, Hyperbola no lower than mid-cone), shortening the leader dashes.

feedback.rationale: Concept, primitives, and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (fill opacity, cone shading, trace extents, label placement), so the generator should refine execution.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional drawing of a right circular cone, shaded in translucent teal with its apex at the top and an elliptical base at the bottom, cut by four dashed lines that each mark a different slicing plane. Near the apex a short, nearly horizontal dashed segment crossing a lightly shaded band is labeled 'Circle'. Below it a dashed line tilted modestly from horizontal passes through both sides of the cone and is labeled 'Ellipse'. A steeper dashed line runs from the upper left side of the cone down through the base and carries the label 'Parabola'. The fourth dashed line is nearly vertical, dropping through the right portion of the cone to the base, and is labeled 'Hyperbola'. Each cut has a correspondingly shaded region rendered inside the translucent solid, so the section surface itself is visible rather than just the cutting line, and all four labels are stacked along the right edge. Steepening the cut progressively from horizontal to vertical is the entire visual argument: one surface yields all four curves depending only on the inclination of the plane. The drawing collects the family of paths that an inverse-square force allows, the closed circle and ellipse alongside the open parabola and hyperbola.

interactions.label: Cutting-plane tilt from horizontal (°)
interactions.teaches: One cone produces the whole conic family: as the plane steepens past horizontal the section stretches from circle to ellipse, becomes an unbounded parabola exactly when the plane is parallel to the cone's slant side (~68°), and opens into a hyperbola beyond that.

interactions.label: Named conic cut
interactions.teaches: Which dashed line in the original figure corresponds to which orbit shape, and that circle/ellipse are closed bounded sections while parabola/hyperbola are open and run off the cone.
The dashed 'lines' are really flat planes slicing a solid of revolution; rotating shows the section as a genuine 2D curve lying in that plane rather than an outline drawn on the surface.

demo_steps.title: Circle — plane perpendicular to the axis
demo_steps.narration: A horizontal plane near the apex cuts a small closed circle. Every point of the section is the same distance from the cone's axis.

demo_steps.title: Ellipse — tilt the plane modestly
demo_steps.narration: Tilting the plane about 25° still lets it exit through both sides of the cone, so the section closes — but now as a stretched ellipse.

demo_steps.title: Parabola — plane parallel to the slant side
demo_steps.narration: At the critical tilt (~68°, matching the cone's slant) the plane never catches the far wall. The curve stops closing and escapes: a parabola, the marginally unbound orbit.

demo_steps.title: Hyperbola — steeper than the slant
demo_steps.narration: Past the slant angle the plane cuts a single branch that opens ever wider — the hyperbolic, definitively unbound trajectory.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cone: apex at (0, +2.2, 0), base circle radius 1.6 centered at (0, -1.8, 0), height 4.0; half-angle = atan(1.6/4.0) ≈ 21.8°, so the slant side makes 68.2° with the horizontal — that is the exact parabola threshold for the slider. Axis is vertical (+Y screen-up); base ellipse foreshortened by the ~12° camera elevation. Cutting planes all contain a horizontal line perpendicular to the viewing axis and tilt about it: Circle plane at y≈+1.3 (tilt 0°, section radius ≈0.36); Ellipse plane at y≈+0.6, tilt ≈25°; Parabola plane tilt 68.2° passing through the upper-LEFT slant and exiting the base near the left-front rim; Hyperbola plane tilt ≈85° offset to the RIGHT of the axis by x≈+0.55, dropping to the base. Colors: cone body translucent teal #7FBFBF with a lighter vertical highlight band #BFE0DE down the left-center and a darker rim #3E8C8C; base disk #4F9E9E with darker ellipse edge #2F7676; section surfaces a desaturated gray-teal #6E9494 at ~0.55 opacity; cut lines black dashed (dash 0.12, gap 0.10, width ~1.5px); labels black sans-serif, stacked at the right edge at descending heights y ≈ +2.0 (Circle), +1.5 (Ellipse), +0.9 (Parabola), +0.1 (Hyperbola), each with a short leader tick to its dashed line.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the cone as a ConeGeometry (radialSegments 64, openEnded false) with MeshPhysicalMaterial, transparent true, opacity ~0.45, depthWrite false, side: THREE.DoubleSide so interior walls read through the shell. Compute the section curve analytically: intersect the plane with the cone x²+z² = (r/h)²·(apexY − y)² and sample it as a polyline, then triangulate (fan for closed conics, clipped strip for parabola/hyperbola) into a filled mesh so the section surface is visible, not just the line. Draw the dashed cut lines with LineDashedMaterial and call computeLineDistances() after every slider update. Unselected cuts fade to opacity ~0.12 with gray lines; the selected cut's plane, section fill, and label render at full opacity with an accent outline. Labels via CSS2DRenderer anchored to fixed screen-right positions so stacking survives orbiting. Clamp orbit elevation to roughly −5°…55° to keep the apex-up reading of the figure.

discrepancies: The shaded conic sections are barely visible: in the source each cut is a clearly darker teal patch (circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola regions) whereas the generated fills read as thin outlined slivers with almost no contrast against the cone shell.

Cone body colour/shading differs: the source cone is a saturated teal with a bright vertical highlight stripe and a dark rim; the rendered shell reads as a washed-out grey-green (only the base disc keeps the teal), weakening the family resemblance.

Dashed cutting-plane traces are much shorter than in the source, where the parabola and hyperbola dashed lines run well past the cone (below the base and above the apex) to convey infinite planes; here extensions are only ~0.3–0.55 units.

Label stack placement: source labels sit in a tight right column with short leaders touching each trace; in the render the Circle leader crosses the cone and several leaders are long/detached, making the label-to-cut association less immediate.
The circle cut near the apex is drawn with an essentially invisible fill (radius 0.24) and reads as a single black horizontal line, losing the 'small circle' region shown shaded in the original.
